title: Applications: From Invariants To Measurements
notes: Open the lecture by making the chapter feel less like a catalog and more like a template. The four application areas look different on the surface, but each one asks the same design question: what function turns messy scientific data into a filtration whose persistent features can support a decision? Point to the source span as orientation and emphasize that the deck uses original toy models to rehearse that workflow.

title: Four Pipelines, One Pattern
notes: Use this slide to establish the grammar that the rest of the lecture repeats. Students should hear the same nouns again and again: data, function, filtration, diagram, simplification, decision. The point is not that every application is identical; it is that a topological application becomes teachable when its choices are exposed in this order and when every cancellation threshold is treated as part of the model.

title: Gene Expression As A Signal
notes: The gene-expression section is a friendly entry point because the data are already function-like. Make the conversion explicit anyway: a gene gives a sampled time course, interpolation gives a scalar function, and sublevel or superlevel sweeps turn extrema into birth-death information. The scientific question is periodicity, but the topological question is whether one oscillatory feature remains large after the minor wiggles have been cancelled.

title: Persistence Simplifies Oscillations
notes: This is the first place to insist on a ledger. A smoothing step in data analysis can feel subjective unless the class can point to a precise birth, death, and lifetime. The toy numbers are deliberately simple: one oscillation is obviously robust, one is below threshold, and the cancellation rule can be checked without needing a large persistence library.

title: Stable Periodicity Measures
notes: Connect this slide back to Chapter 08 stability. The application needs a score, but the score is credible only if it comes with a perturbation story. Here the bottleneck bound tells students why small vertical noise in the signal cannot move persistence features arbitrarily far. That does not solve biology, but it protects the ranking from being a pure artifact of sampling jitter.

title: Ranking Genes With Persistence Features
notes: This slide turns persistence into a decision surface. The goal is not to claim that four toy genes settle a biological question; it is to show how a persistent feature becomes part of a ranking rule. Stress that the regularity ratio is important: a large feature can be less convincing if many nearly equal features remain, because that pattern looks like complicated noise rather than a single periodic driver.

title: Protein Docking As Surface Matching
notes: Introduce docking as surface matching rather than as a chemistry lesson. The topological part is the construction of summaries that are less brittle than raw mesh coordinates. A candidate interface can be tested by looking at how elevation events line up across surfaces. The main warning is that the chosen direction matters, so the pipeline must record ambiguity instead of hiding it inside one score.

title: Elevation From Normal Directions
notes: The key teaching move is to make direction choice visible. Students know how to project points onto an axis, but a molecular surface has many plausible local normals. If two directions nearly agree, small geometric noise may swap the order of events. The artifact records that ambiguity, which is exactly the kind of modeling detail an application needs before a topological summary becomes trustworthy.

title: Curve And Surface Elevation Events
notes: Use this as the docking analogue of the gene-expression persistence ledger. The events now come from a surface sweep, so they carry more geometry than a one-dimensional time course. Still, the habit is the same: do not summarize a surface by a vague shape word when a sequence of critical events can be recorded and compared across possible alignments.

title: Image Segmentation As A Landscape
notes: Students may already know watershed segmentation from image processing, so frame the topological contribution carefully. The raw watershed transform is sensitive: every small depression can become a region. Persistence supplies an ordered cleanup rule. The useful distinction is between a basin that exists geometrically and a basin whose lifetime is large enough to survive the intended scale of analysis.

title: Watershed Graph Before Cleanup
notes: Pause on the phrase before cleanup. A raw watershed graph is not a failure; it is an intentionally detailed starting point. The problem is that not every basin should become a final segment. By turning minima and saddle merges into a ledger, we can explain exactly why one basin disappears before another and where the threshold stops the process.

title: Persistence-Guided Segmentation Cleanup
notes: This slide is intentionally procedural. Read the rows from top to bottom and ask what would go wrong if the merge order were changed. The class should see that persistence-guided cleanup is not merely visual smoothing. It is an ordered cancellation process with a threshold, a ledger, and a final consistency check that can be audited later.

title: 3D Critical Cells And Simplification
notes: Extend the image discussion from two-dimensional basins to volumetric data. The vocabulary of critical cells helps students avoid thinking only in contours. In three dimensions, simplification can remove weak tunnels and small cavities as well as shallow components. The exact same audit principle applies: pair the cells, record the dimension, and preserve features above the tolerance.

title: Root Architecture: Local Homology Windows
notes: The root-architecture section gives a different flavor of application: instead of a single global diagram, local homology is used as a classifier. The window is the measuring device. Move it along the skeleton and the rank signature changes at tips, ordinary segments, and branch points. This also highlights a limitation: crossings and genuine branches may require scale or imaging context to separate reliably.

title: Space Carving And Distance Filtrations
notes: This slide connects root analysis to the familiar offset-filtration idea. The skeleton is not only a drawing; it is a set whose distance function can be filtered. As the radius grows, nearby samples join into a coherent architecture. Betti summaries then become sanity checks for the reconstruction, especially when a loop appears that may indicate either biology or an imaging artifact.

title: Application Design Checklist
notes: Close by asking students to reuse the checklist rather than memorize the four case studies separately. Each application succeeds when the topological object is tied to a measured function, a filtration, and a decision threshold. The final message is practical: persistent homology is not only an invariant machine, but also a disciplined way to keep scientific simplification auditable.
